A fireman carries the lifeless body of a child who was among the 844 killed aboard the SS Eastland in the deadliest shipwreck on the Great Lakes. Chicago. 1915

The SS Eastland was a passenger ship based in Chicago and used for tours. On July 24, 1915 the ship rolled over while tied to a dock in the Chicago River. A total of 844 passengers and crew were killed in what was to become the largest loss of life from a single shipwreck on the Great Lakes.

The Eastland had been chartered to take employees of the Western Electric Company to a picnic in Michigan City, Indiana. This was a major event in the lives of the workers, many of whom could not take holidays. On that morning, passengers began boarding the Eastland on the south bank of the Chicago River between Clark and LaSalle Streets around 6:30 a.m., and by 7:10 a.m., the ship had reached its capacity of 2,572 passengers. When the ship began to list slightly to the port side (away from the wharf) the crew attempted to stabilize the ship by admitting water to its ballast tanks, but to little avail. At 7:28 a.m., the Eastland lurched sharply to port, and then rolled completely onto its side, coming to rest on the river bottom, which was only 20 feet (6.1 m) below the surface. Many passengers had already moved below decks and were consequently trapped inside.

For those unaware of it, there's also a compelling mathematical argument for the simulation hypothesis. It starts with a fairly simple assumption. At some point in the future people will be able to simulate realities that, lacking any perspective for comparison*, will be indistinguishable from a reality. I think most would agree that's pretty much a given. Yet that alone paradoxically actually implies we're already almost certainly living in a simulation.

How? Well at the moment that any species anywhere at any time develops this technology there will now be two possibilities. That you're living in the "real" universe, or that you're living in this simulated universe. As time progresses and more simulations emerge there become increasingly more simulated universes, yet only one "real" universe. If you take any given existence, the odds of it being the "real" universe are simply 1/n where n is the total number of universes, simulated and real. As time progresses n increases with no apparent end. Thus your odds of living in the "real" universe approach 0.

* = The lack of perspective for comparison is also key since it means you can get away with just about anything. Think of how absurd relativity is, that all light always moves at the same rate from any perspective. It's very convenient for a simulation since it means you can never go faster than light and look 'backwards' to see arbitrarily far into the past, but it has equally absurd consequences such as traveling at sufficient relative velocities means we can travel, relatively, into the future. Nonetheless we don't assume this as evidence of a simulation, but simply as an element of reality since reality is by definition what can be observed to be real.
